title: Name any commit: the revision-specification language
summary: HEAD~3, HEAD^2, main@{1}, :/fix, v1.0^{tree}, HEAD^! — every git command takes the same revision language. Learn it once and stop copying shas by hand.
mental_model: `~` walks generations backwards along first parents. `^` selects which parent of a merge. Everything else is a way of asking git to look something up for you instead of you pasting a sha.

setup.run: git merge -q --no-ff -m "Merge the side branch" feature/side

steps.title: rev-parse is how you check your understanding
steps.why: `git rev-parse <expression>` resolves any revision expression to a sha and prints it. Every experiment below is safe, because rev-parse only reads.

steps.title: Tilde walks generations back
steps.why: `HEAD~1` is the parent, `HEAD~2` its parent, and so on — always following the FIRST parent. On a linear history it counts commits; through a merge it stays on the mainline.
steps.expect: Four, then the merge, then commit three, then commit two — never straying onto the side branch.

verify.label: ~3 walks three generations back along first parents

steps.title: Caret selects which parent
steps.why: On a merge, `^1` is the branch you were on and `^2` is the branch merged in. `HEAD^` with no number means `^1`, which is why `HEAD^` and `HEAD~1` are the same on ordinary commits and differ only in intent.
steps.expect: ^1 gives the main line, ^2 gives the side branch tip.

verify.label: ^2 selects the merged-in branch
verify.hint: the second parent of a merge is the branch that was merged

steps.title: Combine them
steps.why: Expressions chain left to right: `HEAD~1^2~1` means go back one, take the second parent, then back one more. This is how you name a commit deep inside a merged branch without ever seeing its sha.
steps.expect: Each expression lands somewhere specific and predictable.

steps.title: Reflog positions with @{n}
steps.why: `main@{1}` is where the branch pointed one move ago — a different question from `main~1`, which is one commit back in history. This distinction is the whole basis of reflog recovery.
steps.expect: Two different commits — position-in-time versus position-in-history.

steps.title: Find a commit by its message
steps.why: `:/text` resolves to the most recent commit whose message contains that text. Faster than a log-and-copy, and it composes with everything else.
steps.expect: The side-branch commit, found by text.

verify.label: you can name a commit by its message

steps.title: Peel a ref to the object you want
steps.why: `^{}` dereferences an annotated tag to its commit; `^{tree}` gets a commit's tree; `<rev>:<path>` names a blob inside it. This is how you address any object in the database from a human-readable starting point.
commands: sh -c 'git cat-file -t v1.0 && git cat-file -t v1.0^{} && git cat-file -t v1.0^{tree}'
steps.expect: tag, commit, tree — three different objects from one name.

verify.label: ^{tree} peels a ref down to its tree
<rev>:<path> reads a file from any commit

steps.title: Ranges, and the two shorthands nobody knows
steps.why: `A..B` and `A...B` you have met. `HEAD^!` means 'this commit but not its parents' — perfect for showing a single commit. `HEAD^@` means 'all parents of HEAD' — the building block of both.
steps.expect: A range, a single commit, and the parent lists behind the notation.

steps.title: Use it instead of copying shas
steps.why: Every command takes these expressions — diff, show, restore, reset, cherry-pick, rebase. Writing `git restore --source=:/Commit two app.py` is both shorter and self-documenting compared with a pasted sha.
steps.expect: The file restored from a commit named by its message.

verify.label: a file was restored using a message-based revision

steps.title: Clean up
steps.why: Put the file back. Every expression above was read-only except this last restore — revision syntax is a naming language, not an action.

verify.label: you can name a commit on the merged-in branch without its sha
you can peel a tag to any object type
nothing was left modified — revision syntax only names things

pitfalls: `HEAD^2` is the second PARENT; `HEAD~2` is two commits back. On a non-merge commit `^2` simply fails, which is the quickest way to remember the difference.
`^` is a special character in Windows cmd.exe and must be doubled or quoted. In PowerShell and bash it is fine.
`main@{1}` is a reflog position, not a commit ancestor. After a reset the two point at completely different places — which is exactly what makes recovery possible.
`:/text` searches from HEAD backwards and takes the first match. In a repository with repeated messages it may not be the one you meant.
`git rev-parse <expr>` is free and instant. When an expression matters, check it there before putting it in a `reset --hard`.
cheatsheet: n generations back, first parents only
the nth parent of a merge (^ alone means ^1)
where the branch pointed n moves ago
the most recent commit whose message contains text
peel an annotated tag to its commit
a commit's tree / a file inside it
just this commit, excluding its parents
check any expression without acting on it
